title: Night Work
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 14 of 40
content:
Snape taught the Patronus Charm like he taught everything else: as if failure were an irritating but unsurprising condition I had personally invented.

“Again.”

A thread of silver mist left my wand and collapsed.

“Your focus wandered.”

“I noticed.”

“Then why did you permit it?”

“Because thoughts are famously obedient.”

“They can be trained.”

“Not everyone stores theirs in labeled jars.”

His expression sharpened.

“Do you imagine Occlumency is filing?”

“I imagine yours has shelves.”

“You imagine too much.”

“Again?”

“Again.”

We practiced in an unused classroom near the Astronomy Tower because Snape said the dungeons encouraged the wrong associations after the Dementor breach. I suspected he also preferred a room with windows.

He stood near the door, arms folded, black robes making him look like a disapproving shadow.

I tried to find the memory I had chosen.

Not my happiest.

He had corrected me on that immediately.

“Happiness is vague,” he said. “Use something specific enough to resist substitution.”

So I chose a moment that belonged only to me: warm light, safety, the sensation of laughter arriving after I had been certain I had forgotten how.

The details did not need to be anyone else's.

They only needed to be mine.

I raised my wand.

Silver mist gathered.

This time it held shape for almost two seconds before dissolving.

Snape's eyebrows rose.

“Better.”

I grinned.

His face immediately regretted encouraging me.

“Do not become smug.”

“You said better.”

“I was describing a measurable improvement, not granting permission for celebration.”

“Too late.”

We went again.

By midnight, my arm ached and Snape's voice had gone rough.

“Enough.”

“One more.”

“No.”

“You sound like Pomfrey.”

“An unforgivable insult.”

“One more.”

He studied me.

“Why?”

I lowered the wand.

Because I did not want to return to my room.

Because practice with him had become easier than sleep.

Because when I failed, he corrected technique instead of making the failure about my worth.

Because every time he said again, some stubborn part of me heard the message underneath it: I expect you can do it.

I shrugged.

“I'm close.”

He knew I was lying.

Not about being close.

About that being the whole reason.

He did not expose me.

“One more,” he said.

I raised my wand.

The silver shape that emerged was still indistinct. Four-legged, perhaps. Or winged. It moved once across the floor before breaking into light.

I stared at the empty space.

Snape said nothing.

I looked at him.

He was smiling.

Barely.

But enough.

“I saw that.”

His expression vanished at once.

“You saw nothing.”

“My favorite word.”

“Go to bed.”

“You first.”

We ended up back in the Potions classroom instead.

Night work had become a habit neither of us acknowledged. The castle was quieter after eleven. Builders left. McGonagall stopped sending notes. The portraits grew sleepy and less intrusive.

We brewed because brewing required exactness but not conversation.

That night we began a restorative draught for Snape's nerves.

Pomfrey had approved the formula with modifications. Snape had rejected two of them. I had restored one after proving his alternative increased nausea.

He had been insufferable about losing.

I treasured it.

“Cut the root thinner,” he said.

“It will dissolve too quickly.”

“Not at this temperature.”

“The cauldron will rise by three degrees when we add the resin.”

“Two.”

“Three.”

He checked.

The needle climbed.

Three degrees.

I smiled.

Snape stared at the thermometer as if betrayal had become measurable.

“Do not.”

“I haven't said anything.”

“Your face is shouting.”

“Three.”

“I can read.”

“Can you?”

He flicked a drop of water at me with his wand.

I stared.

He stared back.

“Did you just splash me?”

“No.”

“My sleeve is wet.”

“Condensation.”

“There is no condensation.”

“Then your technique has produced an unprecedented meteorological event.”

I laughed so hard I nearly dropped the knife.

He looked pleased with himself.

That was worse.

“You're impossible.”

“I have been told.”

The potion simmered.

Snape took the stirring rod. His injured hand was steadier now. Not perfect. Better.

I watched the movement of his fingers.

He noticed.

“Problem?”

“No.”

His eyes narrowed.

I could have lied.

Instead I said, “Your hand is better.”

He looked down.

“Yes.”

“Does it feel better?”

“Some days.”

“Today?”

A pause.

“Yes.”

I smiled.

He did not tell me not to.

The potion needed forty minutes at a low simmer.

We sat on opposite sides of the central table.

Snape opened one of the journals from Spinner's End.

I read a book on curse contamination.

The quiet settled around us.

This was different from the silence on the staircase. Different from the wary quiet after an argument.

Comfortable silence, I realized.

The thought startled me enough that I turned a page too loudly.

Snape looked up.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

His expression said liar.

I looked back at the book.

A few minutes later he said, “You do not need to remain until the potion is finished.”

“I know.”

“You are tired.”

“So are you.”

“I am accustomed to it.”

“That doesn't make it healthy.”

“No.”

I glanced up.

He had admitted that too easily.

“You're getting reasonable.”

“Do not insult me twice in one evening.”

I smiled.

At one in the morning, the potion reached the proper color: smoky violet with a silver ring at the edge.

Snape lifted a sample.

“Acceptable.”

“High praise.”

“It may not kill me.”

“Glowing praise.”

He poured six doses into dark glass bottles.

One slipped slightly in his fingers.

I reached automatically.

So did he.

Our hands closed around the same bottle.

We stopped.

His fingers lay over mine.

No gloves.

Warm skin.

The contact lasted one second too long.

Then two.

Snape's eyes lifted to my face.

Everything in the room became too precise.

The flame beneath the cauldron.

The smell of resin.

The rough edge of his scar above the collar.

My own pulse, suddenly ridiculous.

He let go first.

“Secure the stopper,” he said.

His voice had dropped.

I did.

Neither of us mentioned it.

We cleaned the laboratory with unnatural attention.

At the door, I said, “Patronus practice tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“After the audit?”

“Yes.”

“Night work?”

He looked at me.

“That depends.”

“On what?”

“Whether you intend to continue producing weather indoors.”

I laughed.

He opened the door for me.

The gesture was small.

Almost formal.

I passed him into the corridor.

“Good night, Snape.”

“Good night.”

I walked away.

At the first turn, I looked back.

He was still standing in the doorway.

When our eyes met, he retreated inside and closed it.

I smiled all the way upstairs.

The night work became a pattern before either of us admitted it was one.

I would finish the official audit, eat something recognizable as dinner, and return to the dungeon with the intention of staying for twenty minutes. Severus would claim not to have expected me. A second mug would already be on the desk.

On the fourth night, I held it up.

“Coincidence?”

“Preparedness.”

“For exactly the drink I take?”

“You are tediously predictable.”

“Sugar?”

He shoved the bowl toward me without looking.

We spent an hour comparing damaged inventory ledgers. The work should have been dull. Instead it developed its own rhythm: my questions, his clipped answers, the scratch of quills, the occasional insult when one of us made an arithmetic error.

Near midnight his left hand began to tremble.

He tucked it beneath the desk.

I kept reading.

Five minutes later I said, “We're done.”

“We are not.”

“You've reread the same figure three times.”

His expression darkened.

“I'm not ordering you to rest,” I said. “I'm announcing that my own brain is soup and I refuse to let you benefit from it.”

That gave him a route out that did not require admitting weakness.

He saw exactly what I had done.

“You are manipulative.”

“Learning from an expert.”

He closed the ledger.

The next night, he was the one who ended work first.

That was definitely a problem.
